title: Elena's Electronics
industry_source_label: Consumer Electronics / Electronic Goods Chain Store
fit_question: Tell me something interesting about you that is not on your resume. What would you bring to the firm?
prompt: Elena's Electronics has saturated its store footprint and needs internal growth. In 2017 it piloted separate sales specialists, who handle customer interactions, and product specialists, who manage inventory and shelves, in its cell-phone division. Assess whether the pilot succeeded and whether it should expand to every store division.

clarifying_info.answer: Profitability is very important, but management wants a broad assessment of pilot success.
Televisions, laptops, smart appliances and new technology were unaffected by the cell-phone pilot.
Big-box electronics competitors use varied staffing models; there is no clear industry standard.

interviewer_notes: Candidate-led pilot evaluation. Show the candidate-facing Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 2 on page 147, not the worked solution pages. After the candidate identifies the shift toward budget phones, reveal that specialist compensation is based on unit quantity sold.

suggested_framework.summary: Evaluate pilot profitability and broader outcomes, then test whether results are repeatable in other divisions.

children.label: Revenue, units and mix per store
Product margin and profit per store

stages.interviewer_asks: How would you assess the pilot and the decision to expand it?
stages.expected_answer: Measure per-store revenue, volume, product mix and profit; assess customer, employee, brand and competitive outcomes; and test whether cell-phone results transfer to other divisions and whether staff can adopt the model.
good_answer_signals: Uses per-store rather than only total metrics

stages.interviewer_asks: What changed between 2016 and 2017 in Exhibit 1?
stages.expected_answer: Stores rose from 120 to 160, so total revenue and units are misleading. Revenue per store fell from $300K to $275K, while phones sold per store increased from 450 to 650. This suggests a shift toward cheaper products.
good_answer_signals: Normalizes both metrics by store count

stages.interviewer_asks: Use Exhibit 2 to assess product mix and profit per store.
stages.expected_answer: Unit margins are $300 deluxe, $100 midrange and $50 budget. Total profit rose from $9.6M to $10.4M because there were more stores, but profit per store fell from $80K to $65K. Per store, deluxe units halved from 200 to 100, midrange stayed at 150, and budget rose from 100 to 400.
good_answer_signals: Separates total growth from per-store deterioration

stages.interviewer_asks: Why might specialists be selling more budget phones?
stages.info_to_release: Sales-specialist compensation is based on the quantity of phones sold.
stages.expected_answer: The plan rewards unit count rather than profit, making easy-to-sell, low-price budget phones attractive. Specialists may also lack training to explain premium value, customers may prefer simpler products, or role separation may weaken product knowledge and cross-selling.

Do not expand it as designed because per-store revenue fell 8.3% and profit fell 18.75%. Redesign compensation around profit and customer outcomes, train specialists and study the customer journey, then retest before scaling while preserving any morale or customer benefits.
good_answer_signals: Rejects the current design with quantified evidence
Proposes a revised pilot rather than abandoning specialization outright

exhibits.title: Store and Phone Sales Summary
exhibits.description: Store count, total phone revenue and total phones sold in 2016 and 2017.
exhibits.key_insight: More stores drove aggregate growth, while revenue per store declined despite higher unit volume per store.

exhibits.title: Phone Product Economics and Mix
exhibits.description: Price, COGS and total unit sales by phone tier in 2016 and 2017.
exhibits.key_insight: Sales shifted sharply from high-margin deluxe phones to low-margin budget phones.

math.question: How did revenue and unit sales per store change?
math.answer: Revenue per store fell from $300K to $275K (8.33%), while units per store rose from 450 to 650 (44.4%).

math.question: How did phone profit per store change?
math.answer: Profit per store fell from $80K to $65K, an 18.75% decline.

math.question: How did deluxe and budget phone quantities change?
givens: Deluxe: 24,000 to 16,000 total; 200 to 100 per store
Budget: 12,000 to 64,000 total; 100 to 400 per store
math.answer: Deluxe fell 33.3% in total and 50% per store; budget rose to 5.33× total volume and 4× per-store volume.
math.book_answer_if_different: The recommendation says Elena's had a '4x increase' in budget phones and a '50% decrease' in deluxe phones. The data show budget total volume became 5.33x (while per-store volume became 4x), and deluxe total volume fell 33.3% (while per-store volume fell 50%).

synthesis: Do not expand the pilot as designed. Although total profit rose with store count, revenue per store fell 8.33% and profit per store fell 18.75% as sales shifted from deluxe to budget phones. Redesign incentives around profit and customer outcomes, train specialists and retest the model before scaling, while measuring morale, customer experience and cross-selling.
what_great_looks_like: Connects product mix to contribution margin
Diagnoses unit-based compensation as the root cause
common_pitfalls: Calls the pilot successful because total revenue rose
Uses selling price instead of margin
Repeats the source's total-versus-per-store mix errors

extraction.notes: Both candidate exhibits share page 147 and contain inputs only. The book's recommendation conflates total and per-store volume changes; corrected figures are recorded in m3. Reviewed and accepted by Claude 2026-09-30.
